claims.text: Enhanced resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in HEA multilayer coatings is primarily governed by multilayer interfaces.
Multilayer interfaces act as barriers to dislocation climb.
Multilayer interfaces impede lattice diffusion.
Multilayer interfaces interrupt dislocation motion.
Interface-mediated obstruction produces slower time-dependent deformation than in homogeneous monolithic coatings.
The proposed multilayer coatings have alternating layers with well-defined interfaces.
The proposed coatings have minimal short-range-ordering effects.
Comparing multilayer and composition-matched monolithic coatings under identical constant-load or nanoindentation-creep conditions can isolate the effect of internal interfaces.
An inert atmosphere eliminates oxidation effects during the creep comparison.
Interfaces inhibit diffusion-mediated dislocation climb through local strain partitioning.
Under sustained load, dislocation climb and glide contribute to deformation in HEA coatings.
Interfaces force dislocations to change direction repeatedly or become pinned.
Repeated redirection or pinning at interfaces raises the effective activation energy for creep.
Multilayer HEA coatings will have a significantly lower creep rate than monolithic counterparts under identical conditions.
Multilayer HEA coatings will accumulate less time-dependent plastic strain than monolithic counterparts.
The interface effect should be most pronounced from ambient temperature to approximately 573 K.
Dislocation-mediated creep predominates over other high-temperature mechanisms within the proposed temperature and protective-application stress range.
Stress and temperature govern creep behavior and can change the dominant deformation mechanism in HEA-related systems.
Residual stresses and minor compositional variations may contribute to the observed creep response in addition to interface structure.
Failure to observe either a statistically significant creep-rate reduction or dislocation pile-up/interface pinning would falsify interface dominance.
